title: How to Learn to Draw Anime: A Step-by-Step Roadmap
metaDescription: How to learn to draw anime from zero: what to practice first, a 9-week roadmap from shapes to dynamic poses, a 20-minute daily routine and traps to avoid.
h1: How to learn to draw anime: a roadmap from zero
cardText: A realistic roadmap from lines and boxes to faces, bodies and dynamic poses, 20 minutes a day.
summary: To learn to draw anime, practice the foundations before the style: control your lines, draw simple 3D shapes, build a mannequin, then heads and faces, then bodies in motion. Draw 10 to 20 minutes every day, alternate exercises with drawings you enjoy, and study references instead of only copying them.
heroCaption: A sketchbook page of boxes, spheres and a mannequin: the foundations behind every anime character.
keyTakeaways: Anime is a **style on top of construction**: learn shapes, volumes and proportions first, then the style.
Follow an order: **lines and shapes, volumes, the mannequin, heads and faces, then bodies and poses**.
**10 to 20 minutes every day** beats a long session once a week.
Mix **exercises** with **drawings you love**, and compare your drawings with their model to see what to fix.

sections.heading: Can anyone learn to draw anime?
body: Yes. Drawing is a skill, not a gift: the people who draw well are the ones who practiced the right things for long enough. Your first drawings will look stiff and lopsided, like everyone's, and that is part of the process, not a sign that you lack talent.

What makes the difference is the order in which you learn. Many beginners start by copying their favorite characters line by line and get stuck after a few months, because they never learned what is under the lines. Anime is a style applied to a construction: learn the construction, and the style becomes much easier.

sections.heading: What to learn first
body: Start with your hand, not with characters. Being able to draw a straight line, a clean circle and an ellipse in one stroke makes everything after it easier. Then learn to see in 3D: boxes, cylinders and spheres that turn in space.

Those shapes are the building blocks of everything else. A head is a sphere with a jaw, a rib cage is an egg, a pelvis is a box and a limb is a cylinder. Once you can draw them from any angle, characters stop being flat.
sections.caption: Lines, circles, ellipses, flat shapes and cubes: the first things to practice, before any character.

sections.heading: A 9-week roadmap from shapes to dynamic poses
body: Here is an order that works, in three phases of three weeks. It is the order of the SketchAI program, and you can follow it with a pencil and a sketchbook. Spend about a week on each step, and do not wait to be perfect before moving on: you will come back to each skill again and again.
sections.caption: From spheres, boxes and cylinders to a mannequin: the shapes you learn in the first weeks become the body.
list: **Week 1, lines, shapes and precision**: control your hand and draw simple shapes.
**Week 2, the box method and perspective**: imagine a volume turning in space. See [how to draw a box in perspective](/tutorials/how-to-draw-a-box-in-perspective).
**Week 3, from shapes to the mannequin**: turn a character into an assembly of simple volumes, as in the [anime body tutorial](/tutorials/how-to-draw-an-anime-body).
**Week 4, the head as a volume**: turn a head in space with the [anime face method](/tutorials/how-to-draw-an-anime-face).
**Week 5, facial features**: place the [eyes](/tutorials/how-to-draw-anime-eyes), the nose, the mouth and the ears on the volume of the face.
**Week 6, difficult angles**: stop depending on the front view alone, with the [head from any angle](/tutorials/how-to-draw-an-anime-head-from-any-angle).
**Week 7, torso and pelvis**: understand the central structure of the body.
**Week 8, arms, legs, hands and feet**: build the limbs without drawing them as flat lines.
**Week 9, gesture and dynamic poses**: go from a stiff mannequin to a living character, with the [anime poses tutorial](/tutorials/how-to-draw-anime-poses).

sections.heading: A 20-minute daily routine
body: Short and daily wins. A 20-minute session is long enough to make progress and short enough to never skip, and your hand keeps what you practiced from one day to the next. Use a timer so you do not overthink each part.
sections.caption: Boxes and cylinders from different angles: four minutes of them in every session keep your sense of volume sharp.
list: **Warm-up, 1 minute**: lines, circles and ellipses to loosen your hand.
**Volumes, 4 minutes**: boxes, cylinders and volumes in perspective.
**Technical exercise, 11 minutes**: the topic of your week, like heads, eyes or hands.
**Reference study, 4 minutes**: draw from a manga panel or a photo, looking for the construction.
sections.tip: On busy days, do only the warm-up and the volumes. Ten minutes still count, and keeping the habit matters more than any single session.

sections.heading: Copying, tracing and references: what actually helps
body: Copying and tracing drawings you love is not forbidden; it teaches you how artists simplify a face and how confident lines feel. It only becomes a trap when it is the only thing you do. After tracing or copying a drawing, rebuild it with its construction and draw it again without looking: that is where the learning happens. Our guide [is tracing bad?](/guides/is-tracing-bad) explains how to do it well.

References are just as important. Professionals use photos, mirrors and other drawings all the time, to understand a pose or a fold, not to copy them. Study a reference for its line of action, its proportions and its volumes, then draw from that understanding.
sections.caption: A character from a reference, and the same pose rebuilt with simple volumes.

sections.heading: How to stay motivated
body: Progress in drawing is slow from one day to the next and huge from one month to the next. Keep every drawing, date your sketchbook pages and compare them every few weeks: seeing the difference is the best motivation there is.

Mix the exercises with fun. After a week of boxes, draw a character you love as a reward, using what you practiced. Keep a streak, draw with friends or online challenges, and remember that a bad drawing still trained your hand.

sections.heading: Learn to draw anime with SketchAI
body: SketchAI is an Android app that follows this roadmap on paper. Its 9-week program gives you one session a day, 10 to 20 minutes with a timer, with each week's methods explained step by step. On the side, hundreds of guided anime sketches and lessons for eyes, hair, mouths, poses and clothes let you draw the characters you love with your own pencil, on screen or in AR mode over your sheet.

When a drawing is done, take a photo and compare it with the model to see what to fix, and keep it in your gallery to watch your progress. The app is free to download; a new week of the program opens every 7 days.

faq.q: How long does it take to learn to draw anime?
faq.a: It depends on how often you practice. With 10 to 20 minutes a day, most beginners see clear progress within a few weeks, and drawing characters comfortably from imagination takes months of regular practice.

faq.q: Can I teach myself to draw anime?
faq.a: Yes. Follow a structured order, from shapes and volumes to heads, faces and bodies, practice a little every day and compare your drawings with references to find what to fix.

faq.q: Should I learn realism before drawing anime?
faq.a: You do not need realistic rendering, but you do need its foundations: volumes, proportions and perspective. They are what make anime characters look solid instead of flat.

faq.q: Do I need a tablet to learn to draw anime?
faq.a: No. A pencil, an eraser and paper are enough to learn everything in this roadmap. Many artists keep drawing on paper even after they start working digitally.

faq.q: What should I draw first as a beginner?
faq.a: Lines, circles and ellipses for a few days, then boxes and cylinders, then a simple mannequin. Your first faces will come in a few weeks, on top of those shapes.
